Date: 2025-03-12
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Arielle Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE - lab), Maya Lopez (Lumina CTO), Jordan Kim (Platform), Priya Singh (ML), Ben Adler (DevOps)
summary: Hands-on SDK walkthrough: Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth methods (API key, service account, SSO notes), env configuration for multi-stage deployments, local dev vs CI secrets, and using Redwood Console + Optimize. Agreed next steps: provide sandbox key/repo, run tailored perf script, and schedule POC kickoff.
topics: Auth: API keys vs service accounts vs SSO/SAML notes
Environment patterns: .env, docker, CI secrets, multi-environment configs
Optimize tips: batching, caching, cost profiles
Streaming and type definitions in TS
transcript:
[00:00] Arielle: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We've got about 50 minutes, we'll run through the hands-on lab, show both Python and TypeScript quickstarts, and then walk the console and Optimize bits. If at any point shout out questions.

[00:18] Maya: Great, excited — we want to make sure this fits with our CI patterns and secrets handling, and also how to do a secure POC.

[00:28] Samir: Yep, we'll cover API keys, service accounts, and a quick note on SSO flows. Diego will start the repo demo while I call out a few runtime gotchas.

[00:40] Diego: Ok, I'm sharing my screen, repo is the handoff-lab. Root has two folders: python-quickstart and ts-quickstart, plus a docker dev Dockerfile and a GitHub Actions workflow.

[01:05] Jordan: Quick question — do you recommend storing keys in GitHub secrets or a vault? We use Hashi.

[01:12] Samir: Short answer: use your vault (Hashi) + inject into CI as ephemeral secrets. For local dev .env is fine but never commit. We also show how to use a service-account-style JWT for infra-to-infra auth if you want scoped credentials.

[01:36] Diego: Opening python-quickstart. It's a small script: pip install redwood==0.8.2 (note: version is internal example), set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env and run quickstart.py. Quickstart does a small chat call and an embeddings call.

[01:56] Priya: Does the Python SDK handle streaming?

[02:02] Diego: Yes, we have stream_chat() helper, but node/TS streaming is more common in browser or Node server scenarios. Python streaming exists via iterator API. There's a small example file streaming_demo.py.

[02:20] Arielle: Also note, if you plan to use prefix caching or KV cache, the runtime will accept a cache namespace header — Samir will show console knobs later.

[02:32] Samir: Quick caveat: sometimes the transcripts or doc say K V cache and it's transcribed as K V cash in old docs — ignore that typo in some internal notes.

[02:42] Maya: Ha yes saw that.

[02:45] Diego: Jumping to ts-quickstart. Two packages: one minimal node server using redwood-js-client (we use an internal name; in release it'll be @redwood/inference-js), and a small frontend example showing streaming via EventSource.

[03:06] Ben: For browser, what auth do you recommend? Can't expose API key.

[03:10] Samir: Great point. For browser use, you must proxy requests via your backend. The pattern: backend holds REDWOOD_API_KEY or a short-lived token minted via service account, then backend calls Redwood. We have an example serverless function in the repo that mints a short-lived session token scoped to limited routes.

[03:33] Jordan: Is session token a Redwood feature or something we'd implement?

[03:36] Diego: It's an app pattern — we provide a sample 'session token' helper that exchanges API key for a scoped token with TTL for demo purposes. Not a full IAM service. For production you can integrate with your vault or with Redwood Private's service account flow.

[03:55] Arielle: Let's walk auth options quickly: Hosted API key (quickest), Service account with scoped permissions (recommended for POCs with infra automation), Private deployments can use mTLS or KMS integration for customer-managed keys. Also SAML/SSO is for console access — not for SDK auth.

[04:20] Maya: Ok we need to check regulatory constraints around logs and retention — Lumina logs are sensitive.

[04:25] Samir: We'll send the SOC2 and retention options — in hosted we have retention policies, but Dedicated/Private gives you more control and audit log export. Adding that to next steps.

[04:39] Diego: Back to repo, the TS example uses ESM import style. Few gotchas: if you use bundlers (esbuild/webpack) for the frontend, streaming with EventSource can be impacted by CORS, so ensure routes are configured in console to allow the origin.

[05:05] Priya: Any special type definitions for prompts or structured output?

[05:10] Diego: TS types aim to be light. We provide generated types for responses when you use structured output with function-calling-like patterns. In the repo there's an example of typed schema enforcement using zod. But note: sometimes the model output drifts and you should pair with evals.

[05:34] Samir: Now console: switching to Redwood Console. I'll show how to create a route, generate a scoped token, and see per-route token cost breakdown.

[05:50] Arielle: We'll be a little quick here — important bits: the Console token page shows token usage and latency percentiles, and you can pin model versions. For the POC, we suggest pinning to an L2 or L3 vmodel to avoid drift.

[06:10] Samir: Creating a route "lumina-poc-chat" -> choose model variant rwd-3-xx (example). You can toggle batching and set cache TTL. For low-latency interactive use, set max_batch_size low and enable prefix caching if you have repeated prompts.

[06:34] Jordan: How does batching affect tail latency?

[06:37] Samir: Batching improves throughput at cost of added jitter. We recommend dynamic batching for asynchronous inference and single-request mode for low-latency interactive UIs. In the Console you can set SLOs and the runtime will adapt.

[06:57] Diego: Also mention quantized variants. If you pick a quantized model, you get cost savings but measure quality for your prompt set. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles for target accuracy/cost.

[07:16] Arielle: Quick demo of Optimize: upload a small eval set (we have a sample dataset in repo) and the tool suggests batching and quantization settings and flags regression risks.

[07:32] Priya: Can Optimize run in our CI?

[07:36] Samir: Yes, it exposes a CLI and API for eval runs. You can gate deployments on quality thresholds. We have a GitHub Actions example in workflows/ci-optimize.yml.

[07:49] Maya: That's useful. For our ML team's workflow we want a heathy feedback loop.

[07:54] Diego: Now I'll run the Python quickstart. (typing) pip install -r requirements.txt, export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-sandbox-***, python quickstart.py

[08:15] (background typing sounds)

[08:30] quickstart.py output: "response: Hey Maya — here's a short answer..."

[08:36] Priya: There's a short delay in the demo, is that expected?

[08:40] Diego: Running in sandbox hosted region, cold start can add ~200-400ms for first request, subsequent tokens are faster. Also note the SDK does simple retry logic — exponential backoff defaults to 500ms base in this version.

[09:00] Ben: How do we instrument retries and idempotency for streaming?

[09:06] Samir: For streaming you want to avoid automatic retries at the SDK layer; instead handle reconnection in the app layer with resume tokens where possible. We provide a resume token approach for long responses in the TS example.

[09:24] Diego: Switching to node/ts quickstart run. Node server: yarn install, set REDWOOD_API_KEY and run node server.mjs. Frontend connects via EventSource to /events which proxies to /stream_chat on the server.

[09:48] Jordan: For proxying we should rate limit by user?

[09:51] Samir: Yes implement per-user throttling in your backend. Console also shows rate-limiting metrics and route-level quotas.

[10:00] Maya: On env patterns — our stack has multiple stages: dev, staging, prod — what do you recommend for managing route configs?

[10:08] Arielle: Use separate Console projects or route prefixes per environment. Many customers create a "staging" project in Console and pin to same model but different tokens/quotas. That makes audit and cost reporting simpler.

[10:22] Ben: If we go Dedicated or Private later, how different is the SDK usage?

[10:26] Samir: Minimal change to SDK usage. Endpoint URL changes (e.g., private-hosted internal endpoint) and auth can be mTLS or service account; otherwise API surface is same. That's one of our design goals — same dev experience across hosted/dedicated/private.

[10:42] Diego: Quick note: for on-prem, you likely will use internal DNS names and an ingress that terminates TLS locally; the SDK supports custom base_url. See private-deploy/README in repo.

[10:55] Priya: About telemetry — do you get token-level content? We need to ensure PII doesn't leak.

[11:02] Samir: We redact PII by default in hosted telemetry and provide options for customers to disable logging or set retention to zero if required. On Dedicated/Private we give full controls. We will attach the security checklist with exact retention windows.

[11:18] Diego: Back to code — opening ts-quickstart/server.mjs. There is a helper createRedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, baseUrl: process.env.REDWOOD_BASE_URL })

[11:35] Diego: Note the client supports an override for requestTimeout and retryPolicy. If your CI run is short-lived, bump timeouts.

[11:45] Jordan: In our infra we use service mesh sidecars, would that affect streaming?

[11:50] Samir: Might. Some proxies buffer streaming connections. For streaming end-to-end, ensure the mesh allows chunked transfer and doesn't buffer responses. Otherwise you'll get the full response at once, defeating streaming.

[12:05] Maya: Can you show the Console logs for an example request?

[12:08] Samir: Sure. (switches) Here is a trace: request ID, route, model variant, token count, latency p99 ~220ms, retry count. There's a per-token cost breakdown too.

[12:24] Priya: For cost forecasting, does Console integrate with billing exports?

[12:28] Arielle: Yes you can export usage to S3 or BigQuery for analysis. Optimize also produces cost-savings recommendations which you can simulate before applying.

[12:40] Diego: Now small lab: we'll modify the TS quickstart to use a session-token endpoint. I'll push a branch and everyone can see the change. (typing)

[12:58] Diego: Pushed branch: feature/session-token. The new route /mint-session talks to /v1/sessions on Redwood with server API key and responds with a short-lived token for the frontend. Example TTL 5 minutes.

[13:18] Ben: How do we rotate keys?

[13:20] Samir: Rotate at least quarterly; Console allows you to create multiple keys and revoke them. For automation, use service accounts and rotate via your secrets manager. We'll attach rotation best practices.

[13:36] Maya: For the POC, timeline is two weeks, we need logs, perf, and a small cost estimate.

[13:45] Arielle: We'll provide a simple benchmark script. Samir will run it on your sample workload and return numbers. We'll also include a cost back-of-envelope for hosted and Dedicated.

[13:58] Diego: Running a quick latency script now against the sandbox token — it's synthetic, expect lower variance than your workload. (typing)

[14:20] Script results: 200 requests, median latency 95ms, p95 230ms, tokens per call 120.

[14:28] Priya: Nice. How do we reproduce a higher concurrency?

[14:32] Samir: Use our load test harness in tools/loadtest — it can emulate concurrent clients and prefix caching patterns. We'll give you the harness.

[14:45] Maya: About RBAC — we'd like engineers to have constrained Console access.

[14:50] Arielle: Console has role-based permissions (Admin, Developer, Viewer) and you can scope route access. SAML integration gives you group syncing too.

[15:02] Ben: For CI, we use ephemeral runners — how to ensure runner doesn't leak keys?

[15:07] Samir: Use OIDC provider (GitHub Action OIDC) to mint short-term credentials or inject from Hashi Vault per job. Avoid writing keys to disk; use in-memory env vars. We have a sample GH Action in the repo.

[15:24] Diego: Small gotcha for TS devs: in Node 18+ ESM is default; if your bundler transpiles incorrectly you may get "fetch is not defined" or issues with eventsource polyfills. We include a polyfill snippet in the README.

[15:40] Priya: Anything on LLM evals? We use evals to guard quality.

[15:44] Samir: Yes Optimize can run evals and produce regression alerts; integrate it into CI to fail merges if quality drops. We recommend a small prompt set for canary checks.

[15:57] Maya: Ok sounds good. For the POC we'll want to try hosted first, then a Dedicated reserved node if costs scale.

[16:05] Arielle: Sounds like a plan. We'll set up the sandbox and a POC project in Console and include Lumina engineers on it.

[16:12] Diego: One more demo: showing a structured output using the Python SDK's schema enforcement. (typing) It posts a constraint and the output comes as JSON, we validate with pydantic in the example.

[16:31] Priya: If the model breaks the schema, does the SDK retry?

[16:35] Samir: No, SDK doesn't rewrite the model output. It surfaces the response and you handle validation upstream. Optimize can flag schema drift over time.

[16:48] Maya: Great — a few smaller items: IP allowlist for Private?

[16:52] Samir: Yes Private supports IP allowlist or VPC peering. Hosted offers IP allowlist for enterprise with fixed egress. We'll include the networking matrix in the security doc.

[17:06] Diego: Wrapping up the hands-on portion. I've pushed the session-token branch and CI examples.

[17:12] Arielle: Recap: Send sandbox key + repo, Samir to produce perf script results on Lumina workload, attach security checklist and SOC2, schedule POC kickoff. Who owns scheduling? Maya?

[17:24] Maya: I'll propose times next week.

[17:28] Ben: One more — can you include an example of how to handle cost per route? We need to show finance.

[17:33] Arielle: We'll include a cost template (excel) with sample numbers for token usage and projected monthly spend for 10k users.

[17:42] Priya: Any rough ETA on the perf numbers you promised?

[17:45] Samir: I'll run the script and get back by Wed 3/19.

[17:50] Arielle: Ok thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with artifacts and the next meeting invite.

[17:55] (call ends)

[18:00] Notes on transcript quality: automated captions had a few mis-hearings (K V cache -> K V cash), minor speaker attribution errors (some lines labelled Speaker 2), cleaned minimally for readability.
